record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: What governs the non-linear rheology of biological materials: do tissue models and biopolymer networks share a stiffening universality class, how does shear stiffening influence tissue ductility, what length and time scales control ductile-brittle transitions in tissues, how does elastoplastic tissue flow differ from glassy elastoplastic flow, how much can cellular structure reveal about that flow, and how do cell division and apoptosis modify active mechanical noise relative to passive plasticity?

evidence.quote: More generally , there are many open questions regarding the non-linear rheology of biological materials. For instance, do tissue models and biopolymer networks sit in the same stiffening universality class, and how does shear-stiffening influence ductility of tissues?

What are the dominant/relevant length and time scales controlling the ductile-brittle transition in biological tissues? How does elastoplastic tissue flow differ from glassy elastoplastic flow, and how much information about such flow can be inferred from tissue cellular structure? 259 How do cell division and apoptosis modify the mechanical noise compared to standard plasticity in passive systems, leading to non-linear rheological properties?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider continuum and discrete models of soft biological tissues (e.g., vertex, Voronoi, and active foam models in which cells are represented as polygonal domains with prescribed target areas and perimeters, possibly augmented by stochastic cell division and apoptosis) and compare them with models of semi-flexible biopolymer networks (e.g., athermal or thermal networks of cross-linked filaments exhibiting strain-induced stiffening). Define the nonlinear shear modulus K(γ) = dσ/dγ as a function of imposed shear strain γ, and call a model "strain-stiffening" if K(γ) ~ (γ − γc)^f near a critical strain γc with universal exponent f. Address the following questions:

(a) Do vertex/Voronoi-type tissue models and semi-flexible biopolymer network models belong to the same strain-stiffening universality class, i.e., do they share the same critical exponent f (and associated scaling functions) at the onset of stiffening?

(b) Quantitatively, how does the magnitude and onset of shear stiffening control the ductility of a tissue, measured for example by the yield strain γy and post-yield strain-softening or strain-localization behaviour?

(c) Identify the dominant length scale ξ* and time scale τ* that govern the crossover from ductile to brittle response under quasi-static or finite-rate shear in such tissue models, and determine how ξ* and τ* depend on cell-level parameters (target shape index, cortical tension, motility, division/apoptosis rates).

(d) In what precise sense (e.g., avalanche statistics P(S) ~ S^(−τ), spatial correlations of plastic events, distribution of local yield strains) does elastoplastic flow of a tissue differ from elastoplastic flow of an amorphous glass, and to what extent can these flow statistics be predicted from purely structural (geometric/topological) descriptors of the cellular tiling?

(e) Modelling cell division and apoptosis as an active stochastic source of local plastic rearrangements, characterize how the resulting mechanical noise spectrum modifies the macroscopic nonlinear rheology (flow curve σ(γ̇), Herschel–Bulkley exponent, effective temperature) relative to passive amorphous plasticity.
artifact.status_search_result: These are explicitly posed as open research questions in the active-matter / soft-matter rheology community as of 2024–2026. No source establishes a definitive answer to the universality-class comparison, length/time scales of the ductile-brittle transition in tissues, or the precise role of division/apoptosis as active noise. Partial progress exists (e.g., vertex-model rigidity transitions, biopolymer stiffening exponents, MIPS-like active plasticity) but no consensus resolution.

status_evidence.snippet: there are many open questions regarding the non-linear rheology of biological materials
status_evidence.claim: The questions are presented as open in a 2023/2024 perspectives review.

status_evidence.title: Strain stiffening in biopolymer networks (review literature)
status_evidence.snippet: Universal critical exponents have been identified for biopolymer networks but the connection to tissue vertex models is not established.
status_evidence.claim: Universality-class equivalence with tissue models remains unresolved in current literature.
